questions.prompt: What does QUBO stand for?
options: Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization
Quantum Unified Boolean Operator
Quick Unbounded Binary Objective
Qubit Unitary Basis Operator
questions.explain: QUBO is short for Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization -- minimizing x^T Q x over binary vectors x, with constraints folded in as penalty terms rather than explicit syntax.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the QUBO-to-Ising connection covered in Chapter 1.
options: Because x_i is binary, x_i^2 = x_i, which is why a QUBO's diagonal terms collapse to linear terms and only pairwise cross terms remain quadratic
The substitution s_i = 1 - 2x_i converts a QUBO's {0,1} variables into Ising's {+1,-1} spins
Converting a QUBO to its Ising form changes which assignment is optimal
The per-edge Max-Cut term x_i + x_j - 2*x_i*x_j equals 1 when the edge is cut and 0 when it is not
Ising Hamiltonians can only represent Max-Cut problems, no other QUBO
questions.explain: x_i^2=x_i keeps QUBOs quadratic; s_i=1-2x_i is the exact QUBO-to-Ising substitution; and the per-edge Max-Cut term correctly indicates cut (1) vs. not cut (0). Conversion never changes the optimal assignment, and Ising form represents any QUBO, not just Max-Cut.

questions.prompt: On the 4-cycle Max-Cut graph with edges (0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,0), the maximum possible cut is ____ out of 4 edges, achieved by the alternating assignment x=(1,0,1,0).
questions.explain: Since the 4-cycle is bipartite, the alternating assignment cuts all 4 edges, confirmed by direct per-edge evaluation and by brute-force checking all 16 possible assignments.

questions.prompt: On the 5-node lab graph with edges (0,1),(0,2),(1,2),(1,3),(2,4),(3,4), brute-force checking all 32 assignments found a maximum cut of 5, never 6. Why can this graph never achieve a full cut of all 6 edges?
options: Nodes 0, 1, and 2 form a triangle, and splitting any 3 mutually connected nodes into only 2 groups always forces at least one pair into the same group, leaving that edge uncut
The graph has fewer than 6 edges in total
Max-Cut problems can never exceed a cut value of 5 regardless of graph structure
Nodes 3 and 4 are not connected to any other node in the graph
questions.explain: With only 2 groups available for 3 mutually connected nodes, at least two of the three must share a group by the pigeonhole principle, so the edge between them is never cut -- this is exactly why the graph's true optimum is 5, not 6.

questions.prompt: The penalty term used to fold a budget constraint 'select exactly B items' into an unconstrained QUBO has the form P times (sum of x_i minus B) raised to the power ____.
questions.explain: The standard penalty pattern is P*(sum(x_i) - B)^2, which is zero exactly when the constraint holds and strictly positive otherwise.

questions.prompt: A depth-p QAOA circuit has exactly ____ tunable parameters in total (in terms of p).
questions.explain: Each of the p layers contributes exactly two parameters -- gamma_k for its cost unitary and beta_k for its mixer unitary -- giving 2p total tunable parameters.

questions.prompt: For the single-edge Max-Cut circuit (2 qubits, depth 1), exact simulation at gamma=pi/2, beta=pi/8 gave 100% combined measurement probability on the two cut states and an expected cost of exactly 1.0. At the poorly chosen angles gamma=0.1, beta=0.1, what expected cost resulted instead?
options: Approximately 0.519 -- barely better than the problem's average cost of 0.5
Exactly 1.0, identical to the optimized angles
Exactly 0.0, the worst possible outcome
Approximately 2.0, higher than the true maximum of 1.0
questions.explain: Direct simulation at the poor angles gave an expected cost of approximately 0.519, only slightly above the uniform-distribution average of 0.5 -- illustrating how much QAOA's performance depends on well-chosen parameters.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the cost Hamiltonian H_C and mixer Hamiltonian H_B in QAOA.
options: H_C is built from Z_i*Z_j terms and is diagonal in the computational basis, so it only applies phases, never changing measurement probabilities by itself
H_B = sum of X_i operators; X does not commute with Z, which is exactly why the mixer can redistribute probability between basis states
H_C and H_B commute, so alternating them provides no additional benefit over applying just one of them
Because H_B has no cross-qubit terms, its unitary e^(-i*beta*H_B) factors into independent single-qubit rotations
Barren plateaus are a fully solved problem with no remaining research questions
questions.explain: H_C's diagonal Z-based structure only shifts phase; H_B's Pauli-X terms don't commute with Z and are what actually redistribute probability; and H_B's lack of cross-qubit terms lets its unitary factor per-qubit. H_C and H_B do NOT commute (that's essential, not a flaw), and barren plateaus remain an active, unresolved research area.

questions.prompt: On the 4-cycle Max-Cut problem (true optimum = 4), directly simulated results showed depth p=1 reaching an approximation ratio of approximately 0.75, while depth p=2 reached approximately 0.9999. What is the real-world tradeoff that prevents simply using ever-higher depth on today's hardware?
options: Each additional layer adds more gates, and since every physical gate has some error probability, deeper circuits accumulate more total error that can outweigh the theoretical benefit of added expressiveness
Higher depth always produces a strictly worse approximation ratio on any simulator
QAOA circuits cannot be run with more than 2 layers under any circumstances
Depth has no effect on either circuit cost or solution quality
questions.explain: While theory shows QAOA's achievable cost converges to the optimum as depth grows, each extra layer's gates compound real hardware error on noisy devices, creating a genuine depth-vs-noise tradeoff rather than a free improvement.

questions.prompt: Approximation ratio is defined as the expected cost a QAOA run achieves, divided by the ____ cost.
questions.explain: Approximation ratio r = (achieved expected cost) / (true optimal cost), with r=1.0 meaning the circuit exactly matches the best possible answer.

questions.prompt: What is the 'ground state energy' of a quantum system's Hamiltonian?
options: The smallest eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian operator
The largest eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian operator
The average of all the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues
The total number of qubits the Hamiltonian acts on
questions.explain: Ground state energy is the smallest eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian, corresponding to the system's most stable, lowest-energy configuration.

questions.prompt: For the toy Hamiltonian H = Z + 0.5*X, the exact ground state energy, computed from the matrix's eigenvalues, is approximately ______ (to three decimal places, include the negative sign).
questions.explain: As a traceless 2x2 matrix [[1,0.5],[0.5,-1]], the eigenvalues are +-sqrt(1^2+0.5^2) = +-sqrt(1.25) = +-1.118034, so the ground energy is -1.118034, confirmed by a variational scan reaching the same value.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about VQE ansatz design and entanglement, based on the Chapter 3 lab's 2-qubit Hamiltonian H = Z0Z1 + 0.5X0 + 0.5X1.
options: The true ground state of this Hamiltonian is entangled, confirmed because v_00*v_11 did not equal v_01*v_10 for its eigenvector

A product-state-only (non-entangling) ansatz found a best energy of approximately -1.25, strictly above the true ground energy of approximately -1.414, a real gap caused by insufficient ansatz expressiveness
UCC/UCCSD ansatze are motivated by hardware convenience rather than chemistry, while hardware-efficient ansatze are motivated by physical electron-excitation behavior
The variational principle guarantees any trial state's energy is greater than or equal to the true ground energy
Adding a CNOT gate to an ansatz can never change which states it is able to represent
questions.explain: The entanglement test (v_00*v_11 != v_01*v_10) confirmed genuine entanglement, and the product-state ansatz's -1.25 vs. true -1.414 is a real, measured gap consistent with the variational principle. The UCC/hardware-efficient description is reversed in the false option, and entangling gates like CNOT do expand what states an ansatz can represent.

questions.prompt: What commonly cited benchmark value does the course report for H2's ground state energy in a minimal STO-3G basis near its equilibrium bond length, and how is this number framed?
options: Approximately -1.137 Hartree, presented as a widely reproduced literature reference value used to check a VQE result, not something derived from scratch in this course
Exactly 0 Hartree, derived independently through this course's own simulation
Approximately -1.137 Hartree, claimed as a result this course proved mathematically for the first time
A value that varies randomly each time VQE is run, with no fixed benchmark
questions.explain: The lesson presents -1.137 Hartree as a commonly cited literature benchmark (appearing in Qiskit Nature tutorials and papers), explicitly not a number this course derived -- it serves as the known answer a VQE implementation is checked against.

questions.prompt: The standard definition of 'chemical accuracy' is agreement with the true energy to within about ___ milli-Hartree (roughly 1 kcal/mol).
questions.explain: Chemical accuracy is conventionally defined as agreement to within about 1.6 milli-Hartree, a much tighter bar than being merely 'close' in a loose sense.

questions.prompt: In the 3-asset portfolio QUBO example (r=[0.10,0.07,0.05], budget=2), which assignment achieved the lowest (best) total F(x), and what made it better than simply picking the two highest-return assets?
options: x=(1,1,0) with F(x)=-0.125 WAS the two highest-return assets in this specific example, and it won because the combined risk-adjusted return still beat every other budget-respecting pair
x=(0,0,1) won because it has the lowest total risk regardless of return
x=(1,1,1) won because selecting all three assets always maximizes return
x=(0,0,0) won because having no risk is always optimal
questions.explain: In this specific example, x=(1,1,0) (the two highest-return assets) happened to also be the risk-adjusted optimum, achieving F(x)=-0.125 -- though the separate 4-asset lab example showed this intuition can fail once asset covariances are considered more carefully.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about quantum amplitude estimation and classical Monte Carlo, as covered in Chapter 4.
options: Classical Monte Carlo needs roughly 1/epsilon^2 samples to reach precision epsilon, while quantum amplitude estimation needs roughly 1/epsilon oracle queries for the same precision
This speedup is called 'quadratic' because quantum query count scales roughly as the square root of classical sample count
An 'oracle query' in amplitude estimation has the same real-world cost as a single classical random sample
'Quantum Monte Carlo' in this context only accelerates the sampling/estimation step; the underlying probabilistic model of returns stays unchanged
Realizing amplitude estimation's full theoretical speedup in practice requires fault-tolerant quantum hardware well beyond today's scale
questions.explain: The 1/epsilon vs 1/epsilon^2 scaling, the quadratic-speedup naming, the unchanged-model framing of quantum Monte Carlo, and the fault-tolerance requirement are all directly from the lesson. An oracle query is NOT equivalent in cost to a classical sample -- that's exactly the overstatement the lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: For a target precision epsilon=0.01, classical Monte Carlo needs roughly ______ samples, while quantum amplitude estimation needs roughly 100 oracle queries for the same precision.
questions.explain: Classical samples scale as 1/epsilon^2 = 1/(0.01)^2 = 10,000, compared to quantum's 1/epsilon = 100 queries -- a 100x reduction in query count for this precision target.

questions.prompt: A press release claims a quantum algorithm estimated portfolio risk '50x faster' than classical methods. Per this course's claim-evaluation framework, which of the following is the MOST important follow-up question?
options: Was the 50x figure an empirical wall-clock measurement against the strongest available classical method on a realistic problem size and on real hardware, or a theoretical query-count ratio dressed up as a practical result?
How many words long is the press release?
Does the press release use the word 'quantum' more than once?
Was the press release issued on a weekday?
questions.explain: The course's four-question framework asks whether the speedup is theoretical or empirical, whether the baseline was strong, whether the problem size was realistic, and whether it ran on a simulator or real hardware -- exactly what this question tests.

questions.prompt: In the 4-asset portfolio lab (r=[0.12,0.09,0.06,0.04], budget=2), select every true statement about the result.
options: The naive pick of the two highest-return assets, x=(1,1,0,0), achieved F(x)=-0.0800, not the true optimum
The true optimum was x=(1,0,0,1), achieving F(x)=-0.0850, despite asset 4 having the lowest individual return
Assets 1 and 4 had zero covariance (Sigma_14 = 0.00), meaning they move independently of each other
Brute-force checking confirmed x=(1,1,0,0) as the global optimum among all 16 combinations
This result shows portfolio intuition based purely on individual returns can be wrong once risk correlations are properly accounted for
questions.explain: x=(1,0,0,1) was the verified global optimum (F=-0.0850), not x=(1,1,0,0) (F=-0.0800) -- the zero covariance between assets 1 and 4 is exactly why pairing them reduced risk enough to win, illustrating that naive return-based intuition can be wrong.

questions.prompt: Starting greedy local search from all 32 possible starting points on the 5-node lab graph, what fraction got stuck below the true optimum of 5, and what method reliably escaped the same trap?
options: 8 of 32 (25%) got stuck at cut=4; simulated annealing, starting from the exact same stuck point, reliably reached cut=5 across 5 different random seeds
All 32 starting points got stuck at cut=4; no method tested ever reached cut=5
0 of 32 starting points got stuck; greedy always found the true optimum
16 of 32 got stuck, and simulated annealing also failed to escape the trap
questions.explain: Direct computation showed 8 of 32 greedy starts got stuck at cut=4, while simulated annealing -- using its willingness to accept worsening moves -- reliably reached the true optimum of 5 from the exact same starting point across multiple seeds.

questions.prompt: Select every failure mode this course identifies in unfair quantum-vs-classical optimization benchmarks.
options: Comparing against a weak classical baseline instead of the strongest reasonably available method
Reporting query count without reporting query cost
Cherry-picking a small or specially structured problem instance and implying it generalizes to larger scale
Excluding classical pre- and post-processing overhead (like the parameter-optimization loop) from the timing comparison
Always requiring both methods to use exactly the same programming language
questions.explain: The course names four specific failure modes: weak baselines, query-count-without-cost, cherry-picked instances, and excluded pipeline overhead. Programming language choice is not among the failure modes discussed.

questions.prompt: 'Quantum advantage' has a precise meaning: a demonstrated case where a quantum computer solves some problem faster than ___ known classical method can, on real hardware, for a real task.
questions.explain: The precise definition requires outperforming any known classical method on real hardware for a real task -- a much narrower and more demanding bar than a theoretical scaling advantage alone.

questions.prompt: What is the current honest state of VQE compared to classical quantum chemistry methods like coupled-cluster theory (CCSD(T)), per this course's assessment?
options: VQE has reliably reproduced known energies for small molecules (H2, LiH) as a proof of concept, but has not outperformed CCSD(T)-class classical methods on any molecule of practical chemical interest
VQE has already outperformed CCSD(T) on all molecules larger than 100 atoms
CCSD(T) and VQE have never been compared on any molecule
VQE has replaced CCSD(T) as the default industry-standard method in computational chemistry
questions.explain: The course is explicit: VQE's proof-of-concept successes on small molecules do not extend to outperforming the classical gold-standard CCSD(T) on any molecule of practical scientific or industrial interest.

questions.prompt: Select every item on this course's four-question checklist for evaluating a quantum optimization benchmark claim.
options: Is the claimed speedup theoretical or empirical?
What problem size was actually tested, and does it resemble a real-world instance?
Was the comparison against the best available classical method or a weak one?
Does the claim distinguish a simulator run from a real noisy-hardware run?
Did the research team include at least one physicist?
questions.explain: The four-question checklist covers theoretical-vs-empirical, realistic problem size, baseline strength, and simulator-vs-hardware -- team composition is not part of the checklist.

questions.prompt: For the capstone's Number Partitioning problem (task durations d=[3,5,2,4]), both brute force and the classical LPT heuristic found a 7-7 hour split (F=0). What did simulated QAOA at depth 1 find instead, after a parameter search?
options: An expected cost of approximately 14.2, with the two true-optimal bitstrings carrying only about 0.95% combined measurement probability, while near-optimal bitstrings (cost=4) carried about 49.2%
The exact same 7-7 split, with 100% measurement probability on the true optimum
An expected cost of exactly 0, matching the classical methods perfectly
A result that could not be computed at all for this problem
questions.explain: The directly-simulated QAOA p=1 result concentrated most probability on a near-optimal cluster (cost=4, ~49.2% combined) rather than the true optimum (cost=0, only ~0.95% combined) -- a genuine, verified finding, not a computational error.

questions.prompt: The Longest Processing Time (LPT) classical heuristic works by sorting items in ______ order, then greedily assigning each one to whichever group currently has the smaller total.
questions.explain: LPT sorts items in decreasing order and greedily assigns each to the smaller-total group, which is exactly the deterministic procedure that found the capstone problem's true optimum in one pass.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the LPT heuristic's general reliability, based on the capstone's own testing.
options: LPT found the exact true optimum (F=0) on the capstone's 4-task instance, d=[3,5,2,4]
On the instance d=[5,6,4,1,9,8], LPT produced an imbalance of 3, while the true optimal split ({9,8} vs {6,5,4,1}) achieves an imbalance of only 1
These two results together show LPT is not mathematically guaranteed to find the true optimum on every possible Number Partitioning instance
Because LPT succeeded on one instance, it is guaranteed to succeed on all future instances
LPT requires a continuous parameter search, similar to QAOA's gamma and beta
questions.explain: LPT succeeded on the capstone's original instance but failed to reach the true optimum on d=[5,6,4,1,9,8] -- together these confirm LPT is a strong heuristic, not a guaranteed-optimal algorithm. It also requires no parameter search at all, unlike QAOA.

questions.prompt: Using the approximation that expected trials to first success equals 1 divided by the probability of success, and a true-optimal measurement probability of about 0.95% (0.0095), the expected number of QAOA measurement shots needed to see the true optimum at least once is approximately ____.
questions.explain: 1/0.0095 is approximately 105, meaning on average about 105 measurement shots would be needed to observe a true-optimal bitstring at least once -- a concrete cost figure for the capstone writeup, compared to LPT's single deterministic pass.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the five sections this course requires in an honest optimization capstone writeup?
options: Problem statement, formulation (verified QUBO/Ising conversion), methods compared with their actual results, an honest comparison applying the fairness checklist, and specific limitations/costs
Introduction, literature review, abstract, references, and acknowledgments only
Qubit count, gate count, circuit depth, vendor name, and publication date
Hypothesis, methodology, results, discussion, and a marketing summary
questions.explain: The course's model writeup structure is: problem statement, verified formulation, methods and actual results, an honest comparison explicitly applying the fairness checklist, and specific (not vague) limitations and computational costs.
